lessons.title: Who is a food handler under FHR 2009
lessons.summary: You will be able to say whether you are a food handler and name what the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009 require of you before your first shift. Covers reg. 2's definition — anyone preparing food, touching food or food-contact surfaces, or handling packaged food or appliances — plus the training duty in regs. 30 and 31(1). Prevents assuming the SOP folder is the only rule that applies behind the bar.

payload.markdown:
The SOP folder tells you how Mutiara makes drinks. It does not tell you who the law counts as a food handler, or what you must have done before your first shift. Those come from the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009, P.U.(A) 95/2009, made under the Food Act 1983.

Regulation 2 defines a food handler as anyone who is directly involved in preparing food, comes into contact with food or food-contact surfaces, or handles packaged or unpackaged food or appliances in food premises. Your one-page summary puts it plainly: crew who scoop pearls, pour milk, seal cups or wash shakers are food handlers. That is the whole bar team, including whoever is on the sealer and whoever is at the sink.

The word doing the work is *contact*. You do not have to cook anything to be covered. Touching a shaker, a sealing head, a scoop or a cup rim is contact with a food-contact surface. Handling a sealed cup or a bag of dry pearls is handling packaged or unpackaged food. The definition is about what you touch, not about your job title.

Once you are a food handler, regs. 30 and 31(1) attach duties before your first shift. You attend food handler training and get a Certificate of Food Handlers Training from an institution specified by the Director, MOH-recognised. You go for a medical check and vaccination by a registered medical practitioner — in practice, the anti-typhoid injection. The owner must not let you work without training, medical examination and vaccination, and must keep those records for inspection.

Reg. 31(2) covers illness: if you have, carry, or may have a food-borne disease, do not enter the food premises or handle food, report it to management immediately, and stay off work until a registered medical practitioner certifies you cured and fit to work.

The penalties are real. Most food-handler offences under regs. 30, 31 and 33–38 carry a fine of up to RM 10,000 or imprisonment of up to 2 years. The clothing offence under reg. 32 carries a fine of up to RM 1,000. The summary is not legal advice and the regulations may have been amended since 2009 — check the current text with the Food Safety and Quality Division, MOH.

blocks.title: Four Mutiara roles, checked against reg. 2

payload.title: Four Mutiara roles, checked against reg. 2
payload.markdown:
**Role A — pearl station.** You scoop cooked pearls from the warmer into cups. You are directly involved in preparing food and you contact the pearls and the scoop. Food handler under reg. 2. Reg. 30 and 31(1) apply before your first shift.

**Role B — sealer and cup runner.** You take the filled cup, wipe the rim and run the sealer. You never touch the drink itself, but you contact the cup rim and the sealing head — both food-contact surfaces — and you handle the packaged cup. Food handler under reg. 2. Same duties.

**Role C — shaker wash-up.** You rinse and sanitise shakers between orders. You contact a food-contact surface. Food handler under reg. 2. Same duties.

**Role D — cashier.** You take payment and hand over the sealed cup. Handing over a sealed cup is handling packaged food, and the cashier also answers allergen questions and prints the sticker. Food handler under reg. 2. Same duties — the summary's definition includes anyone who handles packaged or unpackaged food in food premises.

What the four cases have in common: the test is contact, not cooking. If the answer to "do I touch food or something food touches?" is yes, regs. 30 and 31(1) apply to you.

lessons.title: Handwashing and hygiene rules you cannot skip
lessons.summary: You will be able to wash your hands for the full 20 seconds and name every trigger that sends you back to the sink. Covers soap and water before you start work, right after the toilet, and after raw food, rubbish or anything dirty, and the section 10 rule table with its source column. Prevents the two failures an inspector catches first: washing too briefly, and washing at the wrong moment.

payload.markdown:
Two hand-washing failures are invisible on a clean-looking bar: washing too briefly, and not going to the sink at the moment you were supposed to. The law sets the moments; the SOP sets the time.

Section 10 of the Mutiara SOP splits every hygiene rule into two columns: **[LAW]** and **[SHOP]**. The source column is not decoration. A [LAW] rule comes from Malaysia's Food Hygiene Regulations 2009 (FHR 2009) and carries a regulation number — reg. 33(1)(c), reg. 36(1)(e). A [SHOP] rule is ours. Break a [SHOP] rule and the shift lead corrects you. Break a [LAW] rule and the shop is exposed, not just you.

The hand rule itself is reg. 33(1)(c): **wash hands before starting work, right after using the toilet, and after handling raw food, rubbish or anything dirty.** Our house rule adds three more triggers: money, your phone, your face.

Twenty seconds is the number: the opening checklist says wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds. Not "until it feels clean" — count it. Soap, running water, backs of hands, between fingers, thumbs, fingertips, wrists. Twenty seconds is roughly singing "Happy Birthday" twice through at normal speed.

Two rules sit next to the sink and are easy to skip. Take off your apron and cap **before** you go to the toilet (reg. 33(1)(b)) — the apron is what touches the drinks, and it does not go into the toilet with you. And cover any cut with a blue waterproof plaster, then a glove over it; blue because nothing in a milk tea is blue, so a lost plaster is visible in the cup.

payload.belief: Twenty seconds is just a guideline — if my hands look clean and I used soap, I'm fine.
payload.why_it_seems_right: Your hands do look clean after five seconds of soap. There is no visible difference between a five-second wash and a twenty-second one, so the clock feels like bureaucracy rather than hygiene.
payload.what_is_true: Reg. 33(1)(c) requires the wash, and the SOP's opening checklist sets the standard for it: soap for at least 20 seconds. A five-second rinse fails that standard regardless of how the hands look. What twenty seconds buys you is the scrubbing of the areas a quick rinse never reaches: between fingers, thumbs, wrists and under the nails, where the residue that transfers into a drink actually sits. The difference predicts what reaches the cup: a five-second wash leaves what was on your hands, a counted twenty seconds removes it.

payload.intro: This is the wash you perform at the sink behind the bar. Twenty seconds, counted, every time one of the triggers fires.

steps.title: Wet your hands and forearms under running water
steps.detail_markdown: Turn the tap on and let the water run over your hands and up past your wrists. Do not fill the basin and dip — running water carries residue away, standing water holds it.
steps.warning: Warm water is more comfortable but the temperature is not the point; running water is.
steps.check: Water is flowing out of the tap, not sitting in the basin.

steps.title: Apply soap and start the count
steps.detail_markdown: One pump of liquid soap into your palm. Start counting twenty seconds now, not after you have finished lathering. Roughly two slow rounds of "Happy Birthday" at normal singing speed.
steps.warning: Do not start the count when you begin rinsing — that is the most common way a wash lands at eight seconds.
steps.check: You know roughly where you are in the count before you start scrubbing.

steps.title: Scrub palms, backs of hands and between fingers
steps.detail_markdown: Rub palm to palm, then the back of each hand with the other palm, then interlace your fingers and work the soap between them. This is where the residue from money and phones sits.
steps.warning: Skipping the backs of the hands is the second-most-common miss after the thumbs.
steps.check: Soap is visible between every pair of fingers.

steps.title: Scrub thumbs, fingertips and wrists
steps.detail_markdown: Rotate each thumb inside the opposite palm. Rub your fingertips into your palms to work under the nails. Finish with each wrist.
steps.warning: Fingernails must be short and clean (reg. 33(1)(a)); no nail polish or false nails is our [SHOP] rule. Long nails trap what the scrub cannot reach.
steps.check: All four areas — thumbs, fingertips, nails, wrists — have been scrubbed.

steps.title: Rinse under running water
steps.detail_markdown: Rinse from wrists down to fingertips so the soap and the residue travel off your hands, not back up your arms.
steps.warning: Rinsing upward pushes dirty water toward your wrists.
steps.check: No soap film remains on your hands.

steps.title: Dry with a paper towel and use it to turn off the tap
steps.detail_markdown: Dry your hands fully on a paper towel, then use that same towel to grip the tap handle and turn it off. Bin the towel.
steps.warning: Bare hands on the tap handle re-contaminate the hands you just washed — the handle was touched before the wash.
steps.check: The tap is off and your hands did not touch the handle bare.

payload.setup_markdown: It is 7:40 pm on a Friday. The queue is eight deep, you are the only one on the bar, and the brown sugar milk teas are backed up. You just took a fifty-ringgit note from the customer in front of you and handed back change. The next order is a BS01 and the pearls are already scooped into the cup.

steps.prompt: You have the customer's cash in your hand and the next cup waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Finish the drink first, then wash your hands once the queue clears.
options.outcome_markdown: You hand over the drink. The shift lead sees your bare hand on the cup lid straight after the cash and stops you. The whole queue watches you walk to the sink and start again from step one of the wash — twenty seconds you could have spent before the cup.

options.text: Wash your hands now, then build the drink.
options.outcome_markdown: You put the cash in the drawer, step to the sink and count twenty seconds. The customer waits a few seconds longer. The cup is built with clean hands and the shift lead says nothing, because there is nothing to say.

options.text: Wipe your hands on your apron and build the drink.
options.outcome_markdown: The apron is now the contaminated surface, and it hangs over the counter for the rest of the shift. You have moved the problem from your hands to the garment that touches every drink you make tonight.

steps.prompt: Mid-build, you slice your finger on the sealer handle. It is a small cut but it is bleeding. What do you do?

options.text: Wrap it in a tissue, put the apron over it, and keep going.
options.outcome_markdown: The tissue is white and the apron is not waterproof. Ten minutes later there is no tissue on your finger and you cannot say where it went. Every cup made since then is suspect.

options.text: Cover it with a blue waterproof plaster, then wear a glove over the plaster.
options.outcome_markdown: The blue plaster is visible against everything in the shop, so if it ever comes loose you will see it in the cup. The glove over it keeps the plaster dry and in place through the rest of the shift.

options.text: Keep the finger out of the way and finish the queue before dealing with it.
options.outcome_markdown: You finish the queue. Blood has reached the cup rim on at least one drink, and the shop now has a product it cannot sell and a customer it cannot call back.

steps.prompt: The bin behind the bar is full. You tie the rubbish bag and carry it to the back. Do you wash your hands before you go back to the bar?

options.text: No — I only touched the outside of the bag.
options.outcome_markdown: You go straight back to the bar. Rubbish is named in the hand-wash rule itself (reg. 33(1)(c)): the outside of a rubbish bag is exactly the kind of thing that sends you to the sink. The next cup you touch carries it.

options.text: Yes — handling rubbish is one of the listed triggers.
options.outcome_markdown: Twenty seconds at the sink, then back to the bar. Section 10 lists rubbish next to the toilet and raw food: wash before you touch anything behind the bar again.

steps.prompt: It is 9:55 pm. You need the toilet before closing. Your apron is on and your cap is on.

options.text: Go now, come back, wash hands, carry on.
options.outcome_markdown: You walk into the toilet wearing the apron that hangs over the drinks and the counter. Reg. 33(1)(b) requires it off before you go, and the apron has now been somewhere the shop's food must never be.

options.text: Take off the apron and cap, leave them in the locker, then go.
options.outcome_markdown: Apron and cap go in the locker. You use the toilet, come back, wash for twenty seconds, and put the apron and cap back on. Nothing that touches a drink left the shop floor.

options.text: Go now and wash the apron when you get back.
options.outcome_markdown: You cannot wash an apron in the twenty seconds before closing, and a wet apron is worse than a dry one. The rule was never about how the apron looks — it is about where the apron has been.

payload.debrief_markdown: Every wrong turn in this shift shares one shape: the shortcut was faster, and the cost landed on somebody who was not in the room — the customer who drank from the cup, or the shop that took the write-up. The triggers are not a list to memorise for the quiz. They are the moments where the queue is loudest and the wash feels most optional, which is exactly why the SOP writes them down.

lessons.title: Allergens: what the creamer really contains
lessons.summary: You will be able to answer any allergen question at the counter without guessing. Covers the creamer label's four ingredients — glucose syrup, vegetable oil, sodium caseinate (milk), soy lecithin — why "non-dairy creamer" is not dairy-free, and which menu items list milk and caffeine. Prevents the one wrong sentence that turns a milk allergy into an emergency.

payload.markdown:
A milk allergy is not a preference: section 9 lists trouble breathing among the reactions. Your creamer label is the single most dangerous object on the bar, because it says **non-dairy** and contains **milk**.

Section 9 of the Mutiara SOP lists the four ingredients on the creamer label:

| Ingredient | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| Glucose syrup | Sugar, no protein |
| Vegetable oil | Fat, no protein |
| **Sodium caseinate (milk)** | **A milk protein.** |
| Emulsifier (soy lecithin) | Soy-derived, a declared soy allergen |

"Non-dairy" on the tub is not a promise that the creamer is free of milk. This one contains sodium caseinate, so it is unsafe for a milk allergy. The SOP states it flatly: *"Non-dairy creamer" is NOT safe for a milk allergy. It contains milk protein. Never tell a customer that non-dairy means dairy-free.*

On this bar you also handle egg, soy and oats. Section 9 tells you to be honest about that: you cannot promise zero traces, so you tell the customer what you did and let them decide.

If someone reacts — swollen lips or face, trouble breathing, hives, vomiting — you call 999 at once, tell the shift lead, keep the person still, and ask whether they carry their own adrenaline auto-injector. You give them nothing to eat or drink.

lessons.title: Opening and closing the kiosk by the checklist
lessons.summary: You will be able to run the 09:30 to 10:00 opening checklist and the 21:30 to 22:30 closing checklist without missing a step. Covers the shift table — opening 10:00 to 16:00 with a 09:30 arrival — the opening steps, and the closing cut-offs: stop cooking pearls at 21:30, last orders 21:55, discard all cooked pearls. Prevents a bar opened without handwashing and pearls carried into the next day.

payload.markdown:
A kiosk that opens late loses the 10:00 rush. A kiosk that closes sloppy carries cooked pearls into tomorrow, and the SOP is clear that cooked pearls are made fresh every day and thrown away at close.

Your SOP splits the day into two checklists. Section 3 of the SOP sets the shifts:

| Shift | Hours | Arrive by | Runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opening | 10:00 to 16:00 | 09:30 | Opening checklist (section 4) |
| Closing | 16:00 to 22:30 | 15:50 | Closing checklist (section 5) |

The opening shift arrives at 09:30 with thirty minutes before the doors open. That half hour is not slack: it holds the handwash, the uniform, the chiller and freezer readings, the date labels, the first batch of pearls (about 50 minutes), the tea, the ice, sanitising and the sealer test. Skip one and you either open late or open with equipment that has not been verified.

The closing shift arrives at 15:50 and finishes at 22:30. The shop closes at 22:00, but the closing checklist runs from 21:30 to 22:30 because the last hour is where the cut-offs live: stop cooking new pearls at 21:30, last orders at 21:55, and every cooked pearl in the pot goes in the bin before you lock up. The SOP is explicit that cooked pearls, brewed tea and opened fresh milk and oat milk are prepared fresh every day — they are discarded, not stored.

Two failures the checklists exist to prevent: a bar opened without anyone washing their hands, and pearls carried into the next day. Both are invisible at the time.

payload.intro: The opening checklist is section 4 of the SOP, run from 09:30 so the kiosk opens at 10:00. Each step below is one bullet of section 4, in the SOP's order, with the [LAW] or [SHOP] tag the SOP prints beside it.

steps.title: Wash your hands with soap for at least 20 seconds
steps.detail_markdown: Do this before touching anything behind the bar. [LAW, reg. 33(1)(c)]
steps.warning: Starting the pearl pot first because it takes longest means everything you touched on the way in is now on the pot handle.
steps.check: Hands washed with soap for a counted 20 seconds before anything behind the bar is touched.

steps.title: Put on the uniform and take off jewellery
steps.detail_markdown: Shop T-shirt, light-coloured apron, cap, closed shoes. Remove rings, watches, bracelets and pins. [LAW, regs. 32 and 33(1)(f)]
steps.warning: A ring or watch behind the bar breaks reg. 33(1)(f), whatever the shift.
steps.check: Apron, cap and closed shoes on; nothing on your fingers or wrists.

steps.title: Read the chiller and freezer thermometers and log both
steps.detail_markdown: Write both readings in the temperature log. The chiller must be 4 °C or below, the freezer -18 °C or below. If the chiller is above 5 °C, tell the shift lead before using any milk. [SHOP]
steps.warning: Writing a number you did not read makes the log useless: the 5 °C rule only works if the reading is real.
steps.check: Two readings in the log; a chiller above 5 °C has gone to the shift lead before any milk is used.

steps.title: Check date labels
steps.detail_markdown: Throw away anything past its use-by time and record it in the waste log. Use stock first in, first out. [LAW, reg. 38(1)(i)]
steps.warning: An expired item left on the shelf goes into the first drink that needs it.
steps.check: Nothing past its use-by time; every discard in the waste log.

steps.title: Start the first batch of pearls
steps.detail_markdown: Follow section 6.1. A batch takes about 50 minutes, so start it first, before the tea.
steps.warning: A late pot means no ready pearls at 10:00, and the 25-minute rest in step 3 of section 6.1 cannot be skipped.
steps.check: The pearl water is at a rolling boil or the pearls are cooking.

steps.title: Brew the teas and check the syrup
steps.detail_markdown: Brew black tea and jasmine green tea (section 6.2). Check the brown sugar syrup; make more if the bottle is under half full (section 6.3).
steps.warning: Steeping too long makes the tea bitter: black tea 8 minutes, jasmine green tea 6 minutes.
steps.check: Both teas strained into the urn and labelled with the time; syrup bottle at least half full.

steps.title: Fill the ice bin with the ice scoop
steps.detail_markdown: Never scoop ice with a cup or your hands. Leave the scoop in its holder, handle up. [SHOP; ice must be protected from contamination, LAW reg. 35(1)(j)]
steps.warning: A cup used as a scoop can chip into the ice, and hands contaminate it.
steps.check: Ice bin full; scoop in its holder, handle up.

steps.title: Sanitise the counter and equipment
steps.detail_markdown: Sanitise the counter, shakers, jugs and the sealing machine plate.
steps.warning: Last night's wash does not cover what touched the counter since.
steps.check: Counter, shakers, jugs and sealing plate sanitised.

steps.title: Load the cup film and test the sealer
steps.detail_markdown: Load the cup film and test the sealing machine on an empty cup.
steps.warning: An untested sealer is found out on the first customer's drink.
steps.check: An empty test cup sealed flat and tight.

steps.title: Set up the counter and open at 10:00
steps.detail_markdown: Turn on the POS, check the RM 200 float in the cash drawer, put out the DuitNow QR stand, the menu and the allergen board. Open at 10:00.
steps.warning: Opening without the allergen board leaves the cashier without the one thing section 9 says to check with the customer.
steps.check: POS on, RM 200 float counted, QR stand, menu and allergen board out, doors open at 10:00.

Split the sticker into its six fields.

Section 8 of the SOP is explicit: the cashier must stop and explain before taking payment. You do not make this drink. You explain, offer a drink with no milk in the recipe (FT01, FT02 or FT03) without cheese foam or pudding, follow the allergy steps in section 9, and let the customer choose.

lessons.title: Taking an order in Malay
lessons.summary: You will be able to take an order spoken in Malay and write the correct sticker from it. Covers "Teh susu kurang manis, kurang ais, satu" as one milk tea, less sweet, less ice — CT01-R 50% LI — and the "bungkus" wording a takeaway order uses. Prevents writing 100% sweetness because you only caught the words "teh susu".

payload.markdown:
A customer steps up and says six words. You catch **teh susu** and reach for the sticker. If that is all you caught, you will write **CT01-R 100% RI** — and the customer will send it back, because they said **kurang manis** and **kurang ais**.

Section 7 of your SOP gives the mapping. The customer's words and the sticker code are two different languages, and your job is the translation:

| Customer says | Sticker |
|---|---|
| manis biasa / normal sugar | 100% |
| kurang manis sikit | 75% |
| kurang manis / half sugar | 50% |
| sikit manis / less sugar | 25% |
| tak nak gula / kosong / no sugar | 0% |

"Teh susu kurang manis, kurang ais, satu" is one milk tea, less sweet, less ice: **CT01-R 50% LI**. Three facts, three parts of the sticker. **Satu** is the quantity — one cup. It never changes the recipe.

Ice works the same way: **kurang ais** is LI, **tak nak ais** is NI, **ais biasa** is RI, **panas** is HOT. Section 7 also sets the floor on brown sugar drinks: BS01 and BS02 cannot go below 25% because the syrup is what makes the stripes. If a customer asks for 0% on a BS drink, offer 25% or a CT01 at 0% with pearls.

One more word decides where the cup goes. **Bungkus** — or **tapau** — means takeaway. **Minum sini** means drinking here. Same drink, same sticker, different bag.

lessons.title: Building a drink to the sticker in under 90 seconds
lessons.summary: You will be able to read a cup sticker and build the drink it describes, inside the SOP's 90-second target. Covers BS01 step by step in a 500 ml regular or 700 ml large cup, syrup and ice by the sticker's percentages, sealing, and checking the finished cup against the sticker before it reaches the counter. Prevents remakes caused by building from memory instead of from the sticker.

payload.markdown:
At Mutiara Tea Bar, a drink is not built from memory. It is built from the sticker. Section 6.4 of your SOP opens with the rule that decides everything after it: **read the sticker first**. The sticker carries five things you must transfer into the cup — size, sweetness, ice, milk type, toppings. Miss one and the drink is a remake.

The most serious miss is milk type. If the sticker says **OAT** and you pour fresh milk, an allergy customer drinks dairy. Section 6.4 step 1 puts that in plain words: wrong milk for an allergy customer is the most serious mistake in this shop.

The second rule is order. Syrup goes in before ice. Ice before syrup washes the stripes off the cup wall and you cannot get them back. Brown sugar drinks are never shaken at the bar — the customer shakes, after they leave.

The target is **under 90 seconds per drink**. That is not a speed contest; it is a rhythm. Read, scoop, stripe, ice, milk, tea, seal, hand over. Each step has one thing that goes wrong, and the SOP names it next to the step so you can catch it in the second it happens.

Your cup sizes are fixed: **500 ml regular** and **700 ml large**. Your milk volumes are fixed: **160 ml regular, 220 ml large**. Tea: **100 ml regular, 140 ml large**. Pearls: **1 scoop (60 g) regular, 1.5 scoops (90 g) large**. Only the size letter changes these numbers; sweetness, ice and milk type come from the rest of the sticker.

payload.intro: This is BS01 Brown Sugar Milk Tea, built to a sticker that reads: **BS01-L 75% LI OAT**. Large cup, 75% sweetness, less ice, oat milk. Follow the eight steps in this order. The order is forced — syrup before ice, milk before tea — and reversing any pair changes the drink.

steps.title: Read the sticker out loud
steps.detail_markdown: Say the five fields to yourself before you touch anything: size (R or L), sweetness (%), ice level, milk type (fresh or OAT), toppings. Scan for **ALG**. For `BS01-L 75% LI OAT` you say: large, 75%, less ice, oat, pearls.
steps.warning: Building from memory. The SOP states this is the most serious mistake in the shop — wrong milk for an allergy customer.
steps.check: You can say all five fields without looking at the sticker again.

steps.title: Scoop the pearls
steps.detail_markdown: Use the slotted pearl spoon. Large cup: **1.5 scoops = 90 g**. Regular cup: **1 scoop = 60 g**. Drop them into the cup first.
steps.warning: Bare hands on food is an offence under [LAW, reg. 36(1)(e)]. Too few pearls is the top customer complaint.
steps.check: The pearls are in the cup: 90 g for large, 60 g for regular.

steps.title: Stripe the cup with warm syrup
steps.detail_markdown: Take the brown sugar syrup bottle **from the warm water bath on the bar** (or refill it if empty). Add the syrup for 75% sweetness: section 7 gives 5 pumps (50 ml) for a large cup, 3 for a regular. Tilt the cup and turn it so the syrup coats the inside wall — that is the tiger stripe.
steps.warning: Cold or thin syrup will not stick. No stripes. The SOP says warm syrup sticks to the cup wall, cold syrup slides off.
steps.check: You can see brown streaks holding on the inside wall when you hold the cup up.

steps.title: Add ice for the sticker's ice level
steps.detail_markdown: Use the ice scoop. `LI` means less ice: 1 scoop (85 g) in a large cup, half a scoop (60 g) in a regular one (section 7). Drop ice in **after** the syrup.
steps.warning: Ice before syrup washes the stripes away. Syrup always goes in first.
steps.check: Stripes are still visible through the ice.

steps.title: Pour the milk slowly over the ice
steps.detail_markdown: Large cup: **220 ml**. Regular cup: **160 ml**. This sticker says **OAT**, so pour oat milk — not fresh. Pour slowly, over the ice, not down the side.
steps.warning: Pouring fast melts the stripes. Wrong milk type can cause an allergic reaction.
steps.check: Milk level sits above the ice, stripes still readable on the wall.

steps.title: Top with black tea over the back of a spoon
steps.detail_markdown: Large cup: **140 ml**. Regular cup: **100 ml**. Pour slowly over the back of a spoon so the tea floats as a layer on top of the milk.
steps.warning: Pouring fast mixes everything brown. Still drinkable, but customers photograph this drink.
steps.check: You can see three bands: dark tea on top, milk in the middle, syrup stripes on the wall.

steps.title: Wipe the rim, seal, and invert over the sink
steps.detail_markdown: Wipe the cup rim dry with a clean cloth. Seal with **one full press** of the handle. Turn the cup upside down over the sink for **2 seconds**.
steps.warning: A wet rim or crooked film leaks. The SOP says this is how most counter spills start.
steps.check: No drip in the two seconds upside down. If it drips, re-seal before it reaches the counter.

steps.title: Stick the sticker on and hand over
steps.detail_markdown: Press the sticker onto the cup. Give a **12 mm wide straw** — a thin straw blocks on the pearls. Read the order number aloud, then say the sweetness and milk type: "Large brown sugar, 75 percent, oat milk." Tell the customer: **shake before drinking**.
steps.warning: Shaking at the bar ruins the stripes. The customer shakes, not you.
steps.check: Sticker is on, straw is wide, order number has been said out loud.

payload.title: Two stickers, two builds — where they diverge
payload.markdown:
**Sticker A: `BS01-R 50% RI`** — regular, 50% sweetness, normal ice, fresh milk.

- Pearls: 1 scoop = 60 g
- Syrup: 50% = 2 pumps, from the warm bath, tilted to coat
- Ice: RI = 1 scoop (120 g), after syrup
- Milk: 160 ml fresh, poured slowly over the ice
- Tea: 100 ml black, over the back of a spoon
- Seal, invert 2 s, sticker on, 12 mm straw, order number read aloud

**Sticker B: `BS01-L 75% LI OAT`** — large, 75% sweetness, less ice, oat milk.

- Pearls: 1.5 scoops = 90 g
- Syrup: 75% = 5 pumps, warm, tilted to coat
- Ice: LI = 1 scoop (85 g), after syrup
- Milk: 220 ml oat, poured slowly over the ice
- Tea: 140 ml black, over the back of a spoon
- Seal, invert 2 s, sticker on, 12 mm straw, order number read aloud

payload.title: Build the BS01 station card
payload.brief_markdown:
Your shop is about to train two new crew next week. You are writing the one-page card that will sit taped to the BS01 station — the thing a new crew member reads while their hands are moving.

The card must cover the build for **both cup sizes** and **all three milk/ice variants** the sticker can carry. Use these stickers as your test set:

- `BS01-R 50% RI`
- `BS01-L 75% LI OAT`
- `BS01-R 100% NI`

Constraints:

- One page. A crew member must be able to read it in under 30 seconds while a drink is on the counter.
- Every step must carry its own warning — what goes wrong if that step is done late, done cold, or skipped.
- Every number must come from the SOP: cup sizes, pearl weights, milk volumes, tea volumes, straw width, invert time.
- No prose paragraphs. Tables, numbered steps and short warnings only.

Done looks like: a card a crew member who has never built a BS01 can follow, top to bottom, without asking you a question, and produce a cup that passes the sticker check.
deliverables: A one-page numbered build card covering all three stickers, with the warning beside each step
A values table showing pearl weight, milk volume and tea volume for regular and large
A three-line divergence note: what changes between the three stickers and what stays the same
